papers.title: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable to the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens, and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features -- directions that act like leading, spatially coherent Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a ``Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical applied to both model classes. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens . We also introduce of a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.

papers.title: Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream driving the next block's event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and $6.44 \pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves 10.88% test CER on Aishell-1 (9.28% on dev) when trained from scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy: shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with favorable modeled compute and memory cost.

papers.title: Virtual Placebo: a scoping review of control conditions in randomized controlled trials of psychological immersive virtual reality interventions
papers.abstract: Research on immersive virtual reality (IVR) as a therapeutic tool is growing rapidly, with randomized controlled trials (RCTs) now commonplace. Yet the control conditions in many of these studies that claim strong specific IVR effects vary from usual care to active immersive experiences, making it difficult to draw clinically meaningful conclusions. We conducted a scoping review of recent literature on psychological IVR interventions to assess the main forms of control conditions used and their relations to study outcomes. In this paper, we make the case that most of the recent RCTs studying the effects of specific IVR interventions compare active immersive VR to usual care with no multimedia component. This can lead to strong yet potentially misleading study outcomes and can potentially inflate the IVR interventions' effect. Namely, the lack of an appropriate immersive control condition may risk misattributing general effects of VR devices to the specific content of the intervention. In this review, we discuss the implications of these design choices and propose strategies for including a suitable "virtual placebo" condition to improve the methodological rigor and interpretability of results.

papers.title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators
papers.abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.

papers.title: From Heterogeneity to Function: Enhanced Modular Dynamic Range in Hierarchical Brain Networks
papers.abstract: Hierarchical and modular organization defines brain architecture, yet how it supports flexible computation and functional specialization remains unclear. Although dynamic range is a hallmark of efficient information processing, its distribution across modules and hierarchical levels remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that hierarchical-modular networks naturally generate heterogeneous modular dynamics and firing rates, extending regimes of critical-like dynamics with enhanced intrinsic timescales, reflecting critical slowing down, and diverse scaling exponents without fine-tuning near criticality. Intrinsic timescales increase across hierarchical levels, while their dispersion within levels emerges only when connectivity profiles and firing rates are heterogeneous. We introduce modular dynamic range to quantify how individual modules respond to external inputs and show that heterogeneity enhances both global and module-specific sensitivity, with modular intrinsic timescales increasing with dynamic range. Local stimulation reduces dynamic range in homogeneous networks but enhances it in heterogeneous networks relative to global stimulation. Moreover, selectively stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes both global and modular dynamic range, revealing a principle of functional specialization. In heterogeneous networks, modular dynamic range is more variable and increases even in unstimulated modules, demonstrating distributed computational benefits beyond directly stimulated regions. Together, these findings establish heterogeneity as a mechanism through which hierarchical-modular networks sustain critical-like dynamics, generate hierarchical timescales, and distribute computational sensitivity, providing a basis for functional specialization without fine-tuning to criticality.

papers.title: Phase-based Edge Coupling: Modeling Overlapping Functional Architectures and High-Order Edge-to-Edge Interactions in EEG Networks
papers.abstract: Network neuroscience has traditionally relied on node-centric approaches, which are inherently limited in capturing the brain's overlapping functional architectures and higher-order edge-to-edge interactions. The emerging edge-centric paradigm addresses this gap by shifting the analytical unit from nodes to edges. However, while edge-centric models have been established for DTI and fMRI, comparable EEG methodologies have yet to be developed. In this study, we proposed a Phase-based Edge-centric Coupling (PEC) algorithm for EEG network modelling, where edge time series are derived from instantaneous phase differences of EEG signals and edge-to-edge coupling is quantified via normalized inner product. Simulation tests demonstrated the robustness of PEC algorithm, achieving high accuracy (<10% relative error) in coupling estimation and discriminative capacity (AUROC>0.7) against spurious coupling.When provided sufficient data length(>=16 cycles), PEC outperformed traditional Phase Node-centric Coupling (PNC) in both individual identifiability and cognitive-state identifiability, enabling superior characterization of stable individual neural signatures and dynamic task-dependent functional configurations. Furthermore, unlike PNC's hard-partitioned modularity, PEC captured highly overlapping yet functionally specialized modular structures and connector hubs, aligning with task-engaged cognitive processes. Applied to dyadic interactions, PEC identified distinct cross-brain modules encoding symmetric and asymmetric neural coordination. These findings establish PEC as a valid and powerful tool for EEG network modelling, providing new insights into the brain's complex, multifunctional organization at both intra-brain and inter-brain networks.

papers.title: Estimation of the Cyclopean Eye from Binocular Free Visual Explorations
papers.abstract: Binocular video-oculography records separate signals for each eye, yet human visual processing and oculomotor control operate relative to a single, virtual cyclopean eye. This study addresses the estimation of the cyclopean eye during binocular free visual exploration, a target-free paradigm widely used for the screening of neurological disorders. Using eye-tracking data collected at 1 kHz from 113 participants across three cohorts (patients with Parkinson's Disease, age-matched healthy controls, and young controls), we compare two different methods: one based on an Independent Component Analysis and another based on Factor Analysis. The extracted cyclopean signals were evaluated on their ability to preserve clinically critical fixation and saccadic events using both velocity-threshold and pixel-dispersion event detectors, and were validated against references via Dynamic Time Warping. Results suggest that the technique based on Factor Analysis guarantees full identifiability across all subjects and achieves low alignment errors, performing comparably to the traditional Version Signal (point-wise mean) while dynamically adapting to inter-eye asymmetry. Furthermore, the second factor in this technique was empirically null across all fitted models, confirming that a single latent factor fully accounts for the shared binocular gaze dynamics. These findings establish Factor Analysis as an identifiable framework for estimating the cyclopean eye in target-free visual exploration protocols.

papers.title: GenAIT: Development and Validation of an Objective Generative AI Literacy Test for High School Students
papers.abstract: There is growing international interest in generative AI (GenAI) literacy and its assessment among high school students, but objective assessment in this population remains underdeveloped. This article reports the iterative development and validation of the GenAI Literacy Test (GenAIT), an 18-item multiple-choice test measuring high school students' conceptual knowledge about GenAI, with content spanning technical, practical, and human-impact domains. Expert review of relevance, clarity, and comprehensiveness provided evidence of content validity. In a large-scale survey of 7432 Estonian high school students, we evaluated the psychometric functioning of the Estonian-language GenAIT using confirmatory factor analysis, classical test theory, and item response theory. Results supported approximate unidimensionality, broadly adequate reliability for group-level research (marginal reliability = .72, KR-20 = .69), and good fit of a three-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = .013, TLI = .987, CFI = .990, SRMSR = .021). Measurement precision was sufficient for the majority of students but varied substantially across the latent trait, with lower precision for lower scoring students. GenAIT is therefore more suitable for group-level research than high-stakes individual classification. GenAIT scores were unrelated to perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, and negatively associated with LLM use frequency, suggesting that frequent use and favorable perceptions of AI should not be treated as proxies for conceptual understanding.

papers.title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
papers.abstract: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and correlation evaluation make analyses across recordings and parameter settings computationally expensive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation that expresses the matching objective as additive interval contributions and computes t-distance from reusable correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction, sequential local refinement, and active-block reuse complement CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton execution paths. Across seven controlled workloads with two input realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1,730. All 168 optimized executions reproduce complete reference boundary histories and selected state counts, with a maximum absolute t-distance difference of $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four publicly supplied BBBD EEG analysis matrices provide complementary cross-backend validation. A naturalistic fMRI application segments 4,230 angular-gyrus voxels in a group response and 16 participants; the 17 CPU fits total 213.10 seconds. Mean pairwise boundary alignment exceeds a circular-shift baseline, illustrating cohort-level use of the saved segmentations. Versioned results, recording-level parallelism, and optional low-memory execution support varied analysis scales. HP-GSBS connects an explicit mathematical reformulation of repeated computation to efficient and reproducible neural-state analysis.

papers.title: Hodge-Decomposition of Brain Networks
papers.abstract: We analyze brain networks by decomposing them into three orthogonal components: gradient, curl, and harmonic flows, through the Hodge decomposition, a technique advantageous for capturing complex topological features. A Wasserstein distance based topological inference is developed to determine the statistical significance of each component. The Hodge decomposition is applied to human brain networks obtained from a resting-state fMRI study. Our results indicate statistically significant differences in the topological features between male and female brain networks.

papers.title: Detecting absence: A dedicated prediction-error signal emerging in the auditory thalamus
papers.abstract: How does the brain know what is out there and what is not? Living organisms cannot rely solely on sensory signals for perception because they are noisy and ambiguous. To form stable percepts, the brain exploits its prior knowledge or beliefs. Current theories explain how perceptual beliefs on the features of the stimuli (e.g., pitch or motion velocity) are updated by feature prediction errors: the mismatch between expected and observed values. How the brain updates beliefs about a stimulus' presence or absence is, however, unclear. Previous work has argued that detecting absence, which relies on the lack of evidence for presence, depends on different mechanisms than the identification of a feature. Here, we tested the hypothesis that the detection of absence relies on a form of prediction error dedicated to the update of beliefs on stimulus occurrence. Since feature prediction error already occurs in the sensory pathway, we hypothesised that this would be similar for absence prediction error. We studied this absence prediction error in the human auditory pathway with fMRI by measuring BOLD responses to absence of stimuli for which the participants held different levels of expectations. Comparing more and less expected responses to absence, we showed that prediction error to absence is represented in the auditory thalamus and cortex. Moreover, while feature prediction error is encoded in the auditory midbrain, absence prediction error was not, implying that absence is processed by a different circuit. These results identify the neural mechanism for the detection of sensory absence. These mechanisms may be disrupted in conditions like psychosis, where the detection of absence is impaired.
